A1.justification: Both PDFs describe TREND and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Their shared methods and experiments can be matched despite substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original detection experiments on NuScenes, Once, and Waymo, component ablations, and SemanticKITTI segmentation results in Appendix B.

after.justification: v2 retains original detection and segmentation experiments and adds baseline comparisons, repeated evaluations, sensitivity studies, and forecasting analyses.

M1.justification: v1 uses a range-only reconstruction loss. v2 adds an intensity prediction head using ray-direction and point features, plus intensity-error and zero-surface-SDF penalties (Sections 3.3–3.4, Equations 10–11). These substantively change the model outputs and pretraining objective; recurrent embedding and curriculum learning remain.

E1.justification: The four benchmark datasets and both downstream tasks are retained: SemanticKITTI segmentation already appeared in v1 Appendix B. v2 modestly expands the evaluated input regime through NuScenes comparisons explicitly using 2D image priors to pretrain LiDAR encoders (Appendix G).

E2.justification: v2 adds ALSO and Occupancy-MAE, introduces five pretrained comparators into the previously scratch-versus-TREND Once comparison, and adds UniPAD on Waymo and Occupancy-MAE/UniPAD on SemanticKITTI. Appendix G additionally evaluates first-stage LiMoE and Sonata, spelled Sonota in the text. SLiDR is cited there but has no reported comparison result.

E3.justification: The principal datasets, label fractions, and convergence-matched fine-tuning approach remain. Added protocols test 3/4/5-frame horizons, 80/90/95% masking, alternative ray-sampling controls, curriculum removal, and decoder substitutions; forecasting range error is also evaluated (Appendices D–F). The default-budget NuScenes and 20%/100% Once comparisons reported in v1 are omitted.

E4.justification: The original component ablation is retained, while v2 adds substantial tests of decoder choice, forecasting horizon, curriculum learning, masking, and ground filtering/sampling. Moving-versus-static feature visualizations and forecast-versus-observation examples add diagnostic evidence absent from v1 (Figure 3 and Appendices D–F).

E5.justification: v1 provides no repeated-run or seed information. v2 states that main experiments use a fixed seed and reports five repetitions with means and standard deviations for random initialization, UniPAD, and TREND on Once with 20% labels (Appendix B, Table 7). This introduces uncertainty estimation, although the caption inconsistently calls the dispersion variance and coverage remains limited to one setting.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive comparator, repeated-evaluation, sensitivity, and forecasting results. The Once 100%-label TREND entry changes from 65.66 to 66.09 mAP alongside the revised method description, rather than establishing a same-method performance gain. NuScenes 33.17 mAP and SemanticKITTI 31.12 mIoU are retained. Several default-budget and per-class entries disappear, and Waymo results are replaced by aggregate reporting.

T1.justification: New Section 3.6 introduces sufficient/minimal representations, an information-bottleneck objective, a nuisance-variable causal chain, and a mutual-information inequality. This adds mathematical reasoning beyond v1's method equations, but supplies no accompanying proof or established TREND-specific guarantee.

C1.justification: The central claim that temporal forecasting improves unsupervised LiDAR representation learning remains. v2 emphasizes a LiDAR-specific decoder, changes the advertised relative improvement from up to 90% to up to 400%, and removes v1's explicit first-work claim. Segmentation becomes prominent in the abstract, although its effectiveness was already claimed in v1's appendix.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations concerning nuisance suppression, training stability, forecasting-horizon predictability, decoder choice, and complementarity with image priors. Appendix I newly identifies the absence of explicit semantic modeling as a limitation. The pedestrian-shape explanation was already present in v1 and is largely restated.

D1.justification: v2 newly discloses GPU counts, batch size, ego-motion sources, the four-frame horizon, and pretraining timing, and supplies a project link while still promising release. Curriculum epochs and the 0.9 masking rate are relocated disclosures. Conversely, v1's Cylinder3D encoder adaptation, MMDetection3D implementation, and best-mIoU checkpoint-selection details are omitted.

R1.justification: v2 removes the CAD-model pretraining survey and substantially expands positioning against image-prior methods, ViDAR, occupancy approaches, newer scene-flow work, and Gaussian-splatting decoders. It also introduces information-bottleneck literature and reframes the decoder contribution around LiDAR-specific geometry and intensity modeling.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and related-work discussion are substantially rewritten. Once precedes NuScenes, experimental discussions are consolidated, and segmentation moves from the appendix into the main text. The appendix structure is extensively reorganized, with new discussion, limitations, acknowledgments, and checklist material.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column presentation. Figure 1 is redrawn and relocated, Figure 2 incorporates the revised decoder, and new feature/forecast visualizations appear. Tables gain comparator rows, lose or aggregate class-level detail, and are reorganized into different layouts; repeated-evaluation and image-prior comparison tables are added.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical support through direct competitors across the retained benchmarks, repeated-evaluation evidence, and controlled decoder and sensitivity studies (Tables 1–7; Appendices B, D, F, G). These address important gaps in v1's comparisons and robustness evidence. Added resource disclosures also improve assessability. The gains outweigh omitted segmentation implementation details and class-level results, although uncertainty labeling is inconsistent and the new information-theoretic discussion remains unproved.
